# Changelog

Current API version: **v1.2 (1.2.0.739+1846e8a0d1b7d3254ff24edfb3dab9c25d828e7a)**


## 2023-10-06 [1.0.3]
* [**NEW/BREAKING**] Deleted events are automatically undeleted on update! To opt
  out of this, read the documentation for the specific endpoint.
  This is a willingly introduced, breaking change, since it is the behaviour that all
  current producers requires.
* Support for header `if-unmodified-since` when changing events, to avoid
  the 'lost update problem' for single updates.


## 2023-09-18 [1.0.0]
* Versionbump to 1.0.0!
* Updated documentation for POST /search. Next-links shall always be followed with a GET
* Searching on `id` as a string is allowed
* Fulltext search `q` now also searches on performer names


## 2023-09-10
* [**NEW**] Production environment enabled!
* [**FIX**] Bugfixes when searching with `is` or `is-any-of` so that searching for
            null/not-null also works.


## 2023-09-04
* [**IMPORTANT**] Search on string-fields does NOT support wildcards!
  The support has been removed in favour of more efficient string-searches.
* [**NEW**] Fulltext search via query parameter `q`


## 2023-05-11
* [**FIX**] Better errorhandling and errormessage when trying to use invalid units or categories.


## 2023-05-10
* [**IMPORTANT**] The base URL for the test1-environment has changed, before it was `/v1/`, now it is `/v1-test1/`.
  The old `/v1/` still works but will be dropped soon.
* [**NEW**] Support for searching on `attendanceMode` and `access`
* [**NEW**] Since it is possible for an event to be without a type, `Event.EventType` can now be null.
* [**FIX**] Fixed bug in `is`-query. It did not work. Now it does, and can be used for `null` and `not null`.
* Dev1-environment on the way.


## 2023-04-25

* No Prod1-environment.
* Test1-environment exists and can be used.
  * Using actual storage in CosmosDb. The storage may however be wiped without notice.

### IMPORTANT CHANGES SINCE 2021

* All references (places, units, categories and tags) are now verified when being set or changed.
* A valid subscription is required for everyone.
* A valid registration for OAuth is required for all producers.
* `Performers` are now a list of simpler objects
* `EventType`: An event can now be of 0 or more event types.
* New primary query parameters for searching: `from` and `to`.
* New field: `Contact`



# Introduction
The purpose of CalendarAPI is to consolidate all (most) of the different sources of calendar events that
exists for the Swedish church, to make them easily consumable for many different clients and views.

It is built as a RESTful API in the sense that it adheres to the HTTP standard verbs and semantics, and it is using
'resources' as the primary endpoints for interactions. It does not support HATEOAS and is not 100% strictly RESTful.

As you saw at the top of the page, we publish the OpenAPI-specification for all resources and operations which makes
it even easier to generate code to interact with it, and also for importing into tools such as Postman for
testing or just simply playing around.



## Versioning
You will always be able to tell the exact current version of the API by looking at this documentation page which has the version
stamped in the beginning.

We adhere to semantic versioning, and what that means here is that any changes we do within a major version must be fully backwards compatible.
We can add new fields, **new values for enumerations**, new endpoints and new optional parameters. As a caller of the API,
you **must expect and handle this**.

We will not introduce breaking changes knowingly. If you find that something like that has occured, contact us
immediately so we can roll back the changes!



## Logging
There is a complete audit-log of every change to a calendar event. The information that is logged includes, but is
not limited to:
* The producer that made the call
* The user that triggered the change
* What changes were made to what fields
* When the changes occured

The system of course also logs the usual application logs. So if you encounter an error there is a high chance of
us being able to find that error in our logs so we can help you with your problem.


# API behaviour and functionality
## Pagination
Pagination in the API is performed by specifying an optional limit to control the page size, and a continuation token
to get the next page. There is no support for immediately skipping to page X or specifying an offset.

The only way to get a pagination token is by performing a request that supports pagination. The response will then
include a pagination token, or most likely a complete URL to use to get the next page of results, if there are any.

The pagination token is unique to a specific request and is semi-permanent. So if you save it temporarily you can use it
several times to go back and forth between pages you have already fetched.


## Searching
Searching is available for a few endpoints, each having their own allowed fields to search on.

Commonly, there are a few types of fields that supports searching in a specific format, and those are documented below.

One thing to note is that all searches are case-insensitive, both in fieldnames and values.

Please also note that string-fields in the model that are set to the empty string ("") are actually treated like,
and stored as, null.

Also note that all values are trimmed from excess whitespace before being used in a query.


### Negation
Some types of fields supports negation, that is 'do NOT match this value'.

Commonly this is expressed by specifying a leading `!` in the query. So, to include the character "!" as a pure value
in a query it must be escaped with '\\!'.

The following sections will show examples of this in different scenarios.


### 'Has a value'
To make a query that specifies if a field must, or must not, have a value, the 'empty value' `""` or the 'not empty
value' `"!"` can be used.

```json
// Include all items where `fieldname` does not have a value (is null)
GET /resource?fieldname=

// Include all items where `fieldname` does have a value (is NOT null)
GET /resource?fieldname=!
```


### String-fields
All string-queries are case-insensitive.

A string field can be queried with 'is equal to', 'starts with' and 'contains'.

Use `^` to specify 'starts with' and `~` to specify 'contains'.

```json
// Include all items where `stringfield` is equal to 'some string value with spaces'
GET /resource?stringfield=some string value with spaces

// Include all items where `stringfield` starts with the value 'some string':
GET /resource?stringfield=^some string

// Include all items where `stringfield` contains the value 'string value'
GET /resource?stringfield=~string value
```

(Wildcards has been removed since 2023-09-04 and most likely will not be in the future either.)


```json
// Include all items where `stringfield` starts with 'uppsala',
// then contains zero or more characters, then 'strand', then again zero or more characters (this last part is implicit)
GET /resource?stringfield=^uppsala%strand

// Include all items where `stringfield` contains 'uppsala'
// which is then followed by zero or more characters, then 'strand', then again zero or more characters (this last part is implicit)
GET /resource?stringfield=~uppsala%strand

// Include all items where `stringfield` contains '99%'
GET /resource?stringfield=~99[%]
```





#### Negation
You can also negate the query with `!`:

```json
// Include all items where `stringfield` is NOT exactly equal to 'Some string value with spaces'
GET /resource?stringfield=!Some string value with spaces

// Include all items where `stringfield` does NOT start with the value 'Some string'
GET /resource?stringfield=!^Some string

// Include all items where `stringfield` does NOT contain the value 'string value'
GET /resource?stringfield=!~string value
```


#### Match the pure value
If you need to match a '^' or a '~' at the beginning of a string you need to escape it with a backslash. The same is
true for any negation.

```json
// Include all items where `stringfield` is exactly equal to '^Some string value with spaces'
GET /resource?stringfield=\^Some string value with spaces

// Include all items where `stringfield` is exactly equal to the value '!~Some string'
GET /resource?stringfield=\!~Some string
```


### Ranges
Some fields such as numbers and datetimes supports open-ended ranges. The syntax is
`value-` to match 'equals to or bigger than', and `-value` to match 'equals to or less than'.

```json
// Include all items where `numberfield` is equal to or less than 500
GET /resource?numberfield=-500

// Include all items where `datetimefield` is equal to or larger than '2021-03-10T12:14:00' (using offset in Sweden at that date)
GET /resource?datetimefield=2021-03-10T12:14:00-
```

Ranges does not support negation.


### 'Is any of'
Some fields, most notably ids of some sort, supports a list of values where only one needs to match. Each value is separated with
a comma, or by specifying the field several times in the query.

```json
// Include all items where `idnumberfield` is equal to 5 OR equal to 10 OR equal to 42
GET /resource?idnumberfield=5,10&idnumberfield=42

// Include all items where `idfield` is equal to abc123 OR equal to cba321
GET /resource?idfield=abc123,cba321
```

Fields that supports 'Is any of' also supports searching on null/no values. If you specify a query such
as `/resource?idnumberfield=` you will get all events that does not have any value on `idnumberfield`, and the
reverse for `/resource?idnumberfield=!`.


### 'Is of type'
A few models supports the notion of 'is of type'. The syntax for such a query is similar to 'Is any of':

```json
// Include all items where their type is 'Meeting' or 'Coffebreak' or 'Vaction'
GET /resource?is=meeting&is=coffebreak,vacation
```

'Is of type' also supports searching on null/no values, just as 'Is any of', with the same semantics.


## NULL in fields
If a field on an item has the value `null`, that field will not be present in the *response from* the API. This
minimizes the amount of data needed to represent an item, which is mostly a good thing.

When `null` is explicitly set on a field in a *request to* the API, to create or edit an object, the semantic meaning
is 'remove this field from storage'. So if you wish to remove all tags from an event, you can simply send the following:

```json
{
  "tags": null
}
```


## Date and time
All fields that carries a date and time is represented as a string in full ISO8601-format: `YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss.nnn+hh:mm`

The format may be different in values *sent to* the API. But they are always expanded into the full format, and stored
as such. That means that when they are *returned from* the API, they are in full format, including explicit offset.

## Lists
Even when updating an object, any lists are **replaced** entirely.

This means that you cannot just add or remove a single item, you always have to replace the lists contents. Note that you can skip sending
the field to not do any changes on it. But beware, as previously stated, if you set a field to NULL, that will empty the field.

## Automatic purge of old events
An event is automatically removed from the database around 700 days after it was last saved.

An events history is automatically removed from the database around 900 days after it was last saved.

NOTE: An event is only saved if there are any changes. If you send an upsert/overwrite/update that does not
change anything, nothing is saved and the TTL is therefore **not** extended.



## Error handling
All (well, most) errors that are returned from the API from all endpoints returns the error information in
a common format that is based on RFC7807: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7807

It looks like this:
```json
{
    "type": "TypeOfError", //  AuthorizationFailed, InvalidArgument, AlreadyExists, etc etc
    "title": "A short description for this type of error",
    "timestamp": "The servertime when the error message was constructed",
    "detail": "May contain information about how to resolve the problem that occured",
    "status": 400, // The http status code
    "traceId": "value-of-traceId", // The same value is also returned in the response header `traceresponse`.
    "instanceName": "Name-of-the-environment-and-instance-that-produced-the-response", // The same value is also returned in the response header `instancename`.
    "errors": { // If applicable, all errors are listed with a name and one or more error descriptions
      "field1": ["Description for error in field1", "Another error that occured for field1"],
      "some-other-error": ["Description for another error that also occured"]
    }
}
```
The `type` will have one of a few predetermined values. The API-framework may however in some extraordinary
corner-cases return some other type than those we have specified.

The types that we have specified are always listed in the docs for the endpoint that returns them.

Be sure to always log the response returned from the API at an error. If that is not possible, try to at least save
or display the value of `traceId`, `instanceName` and `timestamp`, as these values combined will make it really easy to find your
error in our logs.

As you can see, we have support for [Trace context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/).

Per the spec we also handle incoming trace contexts. Additionally, we also return the HTTP header for trace context in the response as header `traceresponse`.



# The event model
There are some important things to know when it comes to dealing with the event model in the API.

For consumers, all fields that are marked as `required`, this means that they will always have a value.


## Source and owner of an event
An event always has an owner, a so called 'Unit'. This is reflected in the field `owner.id`.

If you need to get more information about the owner of an event, the master source for units are
located here for TEST: [https://api-t.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Enheter%20V2](https://api-t.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Enheter%20V2)

And located here for PROD: [https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Enheter%20V2](https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Enheter%20V2)

An event must also come from a registered source.

Each new calendar source must be registered and associated with a specific producer (caller). It is then only that
specific producer that is allowed to create and edit events from that source.

In practice, this means that when creating an event you _must_ specify the id of the source, and the id of the owning unit:

```json
{
  "owner": {
    "sourceId": "the-registered-source",
    "id": "the-id-of-the-owning-unit"
  }
}
```

The value will be validated, and if it is invalid the operation will fail.

The `owner`-object contains more fields, but they are filled automatically when needed.




## The place of an event
Each event _may_ be connected to a real, registered place. This is reflected by having a non-null value for `place`.

It is highly recommended, but not required, to add information about a registered place for each event.

If no registered place is connected to the event, the `description` may contain information about where the
event takes place.

Other, more detailed information such as what room the event occurs in, may be found in the `description`.

**Please note** that events that are not connected to a real, registered place will not be discoverable by geographic position.
A common use-case for discovering events "nearby" is to find all places nearby, and then discover events that occurs at one
of these plases. Without a connection to a real, registered place, this kind of query will not be possible.

If an event is connected to a real, registered place, you get more information about it from the master source for places, PlatserAPI v4 TEST:
https://api-t.svenskakyrkan.se/platser/v4/doc

And here for PROD: https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/platser/v4/doc

In practice, this means that when creating an event you _really should_ specify the id of the place:

```json
{
  "place": {
    "id": "the-id-of-the-place"
  }
}
```

The value will be validated, and if it is invalid (the place does not exist) the operation will fail.

The `place`-object contains more fields, but they are filled automatically when needed.

### Brief example of how to fetch suiting places
*Observe that you must add your authentication to the request below, as appropriate*

```json
// Get all places that are owned by a specific unit/project:
GET https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/platser/v4/place?owner_id=2215
```
In the response there is a field named `Id` for each place. This is the field to use as `place.id` for an event.



## Categories and tags
An event can, and often is, categorised with categories, or 'gemensamma ämnesområden' as they are commonly
called.

Tags, or 'lokala ämnesområden' are also used as needed.

The master source for categories and tags can be found here for TEST:
[https://api-t.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Kategorier%20och%20Taggar%20V2](https://api-t.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Kategorier%20och%20Taggar%20V2)

And here for PROD: [https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Kategorier%20och%20Taggar%20V2](https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/index.html?urls.primaryName=Kategorier%20och%20Taggar%20V2)

When creating or editing an event, you only need to specify the id of the category of tag:

```json
{
  "categories": [
    { "id": "id-of-category-1" },
    { "id": "id-of-category-2" }
  ],
  "tags": [
    { "id": "id-of-tag-1" },
    { "id": "id-of-tag-2" }
  ]
}
```

The values will be validated, and if any of them are invalid the operation will fail.

**Please note** that both categories and tags are in a [list](#section/API-behaviour-and-functionality/Lists).


### Brief examples for fetching relevant categories and tags
*Observe that you must add your authentication to the request below, as appropriate*

```json
// Fetch all categories that exists
GET https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/api-v2/odata/categories?$select=id, name, description
```
In the response there is a field named `id`. This is the field to use as `categories[].id` for an event.

```json
// To fetch all tags for a specific unit/project (with a certain name [will be changed])
GET https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/externwebb/api-v2/odata/tags(unitId=2147483529, name='Svenska kyrkans filmpris')
```
In the response there is a field named `id`. This is the field to use as `tags[].id` for an event.



# Event collections
Recurring events, linked events, stuff that happens each sunday every other month. Call it what you will.
We call it 'Event collections'.

At it's most basic, an event collection is several events that has the same value for `collectionId`. Any event can be
added to, or removed from, an event collection. Simply by changing the value on `collectionId`.

The purpose of event collections is basically to make it easy to fetch related events in a simple request.

They are documented in more detail under the endpoint for event collections.

The purpose of event collections, from a producers point of view, is to make it easy to create then with a single request, and to update all of them
with a simple patch. And of course, to be able to remove them all in one sweep.

By specifying an [iCalendar recurrence rule](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5545#section-3.3.10) you can create a new
collection automatically. This is documented in more detail under the endpoint for event collections.



# Current caveats!
If you get `405 Method not allowed` you may be trying to perform a `GET` instead of a `POST`, for example. This
can happen if you try to get an event with a specific id, but accidentally do not send an id. You will then hit the
endpoint for creating an event, which does not support `GET`.

put.description:
Completely overwrite an existing event. The only values that are kept from the existing event are
`Created`, `CreatedBy` and the history of the event.

Note: If a deleted event is overwritten, it will no longer be marked as deleted.
To avoid this, use `doNotRevive=true`.

The data you can specify is a subset of the `Event`-model, the same as for 'Create or upsert an event'.

If you send any properties that are not allowed in this subset, you will get an error.

However, if you need to be able to send extra properties, you can specify `ignoreAdditionalProperties=true` to
explicitly opt-out of the validation for invalid properties.

By default, the resulting event is not returned in full in the response, only a minimal representation. You also get a
`Location`-header you can use to fetch the event if you need its full representation.

```json
// This is the default response when overwriting an event
...
Location: https://api.svenskakyrkan.se/calendar/v1/event/8957ae87bedf491cbb3998e93dc70472
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

{
    "status": "Ok",
    "result": {
        "id": "8957ae87bedf491cbb3998e93dc70472",
        "additionalId": "ABC123",
        "collectionId": "8957ae87bedf491cbb3998e93dc70472"
    }
}
```

If you need to get the complete event-object in the response instead of just the default, you can specify `returnCompleteResultObject=true`.

Either use `include=deleted` to include both deleted and non-deleted events, or use `deleted=!` to explicitly
_only_ include deleted events.

**NOTE:** All date-time values in a query that are specified without explicit offset are assumed to be in Swedish offset for the
specified date.

### 'from' and 'to'
`from` and `to` are special query parameters used to search for events _active_ during a specific time or period.
Both are optional and can be combined with other search parameters.

They can both either be specified as an exact date and / or time, or as a dynamic value.

#### Specify an exact date and / or time
The format is ISO8601/RFC3339, with some values optional:
```json
YYYY-MM-DD[Thh:mm[:ss[.nnn]]][(Z|((+|-)hh:mm))]
```    
Examples:
```json
// Get events active at 8:00 on 24th december 2021, or later (defaulting to Swedish offset at dec 24th).
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24T08:00

// Get events active at 8:00 on 17th march 2021, or later, in some parts of Canada (places that uses that offset).
GET /event/search?from=2021-03-17T08:00:00-05:00

// Get events active between 0:00 on 6th june 2021 and 0:00 on 7th june (defaulting to Swedish offset).
GET /event/search?from=2021-06-06&to=2021-06-07

GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24+04:30
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24-04:30
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24T03:05
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24T03:05-12:00
```

#### Specify a dynamic value
A dynamic value consists of a variable name, and an optional offset.

The offset is specified with `((+|-)hh:mm)`. 

* `now[offset]` : Date resolves to the current date, at the current time for the specified offset.
* `today[offset]` : Date resolves to the current date, at 00:00 for the specified offset.
* `thisweek[offset]` : Date resolves to the monday of the current week, at 00:00 for the specified offset.
* `{duration}[offset]` : Date resolves to a relative date and time in the future

```json
3w5h = 3 weeks, 5 hours
37d = 37 days

```

Example:
```json
/// Get events active today or later
GET /event/search?from=today

/// Get events active only today.

Get events that are active at the start of this week or during the next 10 days from today.
```

```json
// Get events that are active between 4 and 8 days from now
```

further.

Please [read the section on searching](#section/API-behaviour-and-functionality/Searching) for information about syntax for different field types.

post.description:
This resource creates new events out of event data and a recurrence rule in the format of [iCalendar RFC5545](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5545#section-3.3.10),
and connects them together via a common `collectionId`.

Note: See the parameter `doPreview` if you wish to test rules without saving events.

The recurrence rule *must* be limited; you cannot create an event collection that goes on forever.

`start` and `end` from the event data is used to calculate start and end for all events that will be created.

If `collectionId` in the event data has a value, all events will be added to that collection. If no value has been specified,
a new collection is created.

**Note** that the same validation applies as when [creating a single event](#operation/Create%20and%20modify%20events).
### Example
Create events that occurs 10 days in a row:
```json
POST /eventcollection/FREQ=DAILY;INTERVAL=1;COUNT=10
body {
    "title": "en titel",
    "description": "en beskrivning",
    "start": "2019-11-15T11:30:00.000+01:00",
    "end": "2019-11-15T13:45:00.000+01:00",
    ... 
}
```
10 events are created:
* The first event starts at `2019-11-15T11:30:00.000+01:00` and ends at `2019-11-15T13:45:00.000+01:00`
* The second event starts at `2019-11-16T11:30:00.000+01:00` and ends at `2019-11-16T13:45:00.000+01:00`
* The last event starts at `2019-11-24T11:30:00.000+01:00` and ends at `2019-11-24T13:45:00.000+01:00`

All of them gets the same collection id.

### Response data
If successful, the response contains a small subset of the fields for each event.

A `Location`-header is also included that points to the resource where you can fetch the complete collection:
[Fetch all events in a collection](../doc#operation/eventcollection.get).

Similar to the response from 'Fetch all events in a collection', a Link-header is returned with values for
each created event. The difference being that in the former case, any existing events in the collection are
also returned, whereas only the newly created events are returned from this resource.

### Rule examples
```
// Every day from now, for 10 days
FREQ=DAILY;INTERVAL=1;COUNT=10
    
// Every other monday, 10 times (for 20 weeks)
FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2;BYDAY=MO;COUNT=10
    
// Monday and thursday, every week, until 2019-12-31
FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=1;BYDAY=MO,TH;UNTIL=2019-12-31T10:00:00.000+01:00
 
// The first of every month, until 2021-11-18 (last occurrence 2021-11-01)
FREQ=MONTHLY;INTERVAL=1;BYMONTHDAY=1;UNTIL=2021-11-18T11:00:00.000+01:00
    
// INVALID, is not limited
FREQ=DAILY;INTERVAL=1
```

```json
// More examples, all valid, you'll have to guess what they do
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24+04:30
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24-04:30
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24T03:05
GET /event/search?from=2021-12-24T03:05-12:00
```

#### Specify a dynamic value
A dynamic value consists of a variable name, and an optional offset.

The offset is specified with `((+|-)hh:mm)`. 

* `now[offset]` : Date resolves to the current date, at the current time for the specified offset.
* `today[offset]` : Date resolves to the current date, at 00:00 for the specified offset.
* `thisweek[offset]` : Date resolves to the monday of the current week, at 00:00 for the specified offset.
* `{duration}[offset]` : Date resolves to a relative date and time in the future

`{duration}` specifies a duration in weeks, days and hours where each part is optional: `[Xw][Yd][Zh]`. For example:
```json
1w2d4h = 1 week, 2 days, 4 hours
3w5h = 3 weeks, 5 hours
37d = 37 days

```
This is particularly useful to use as a value for `from` or `to`, as it resolves to a value relative from now.

Example:
```json
/// Get events active today or later
GET /event/search?from=today

/// Get events active only today.
GET /event/search?from=today&to=1d

Get events that are active at the start of this week or during the next 10 days from today.
GET /event/search?from=thisweek&to=10d
            
```

### 'duration' instead of 'to'
Instead of specifying a `{duration}` for the `to` parameter, which resolves to a value from now,
you can use the special-case parameter aptly named `duration`. It allows only a `{duration}` value (no timezone),
and resolves to a value relative to the `from` parameter, which in that case must be specified.
The resolved value is then used as the value for `to`.

**Note:** If you specify both the `duration` parameter and the `to` parameter, you will get an error.

Examples:
```json
// Get events active during this week, in the offset used in some parts of Canada
GET /event/search?from=thisweek-05:00&duration=1w

// Get events that are active between 4 and 8 days from now
GET /event/search?from=4d&duration=4d

// Get events active on 18th June any time between 12:00 - 17:00
GET /event/search?from=2021-06-18T12:00&duration=5h
```

### Other filters
See the docs for each field below to see how you can filter on them as well. Each filter restricts the query
further.

Please [read the section on searching](#section/API-behaviour-and-functionality/Searching) for information about syntax for different field types.

#### Examples
```json
// Get events active right now or later, at one of these three places
GET /event/search?from=now&place_id=abc654,abc1065&place_id=abc2567

// Get events active right now or later, for owner with id 2215 and category abc123 or abc256
GET /event/search?from=now&owner_id=2215&category_id=abc123,abc256

// Get events active today or later, at place with id abc654
GET /event/search?from=today&place_id=abc654
```
